frames.source: Source: Ukrainian school atlas map (© Мапа); Magyars, Bulgarian Empire and Khazar extent added from The World Through Time (880). Tribes are not areas.

frames.source: Sources: 'Kievan Rus, 880–1054' map; 862–912 atlas map; Magyars, Bulgaria, Khazars from The World Through Time (895). Peoples' names not territory.

frames.title: Rus' after the expansion of c.912–972
frames.source: 'Kievan Rus, 880–1054' map; west contested, no state drawn; steppe and N. Crimea Pecheneg after the Khazar collapse (c. 965). Peoples' names are placed where the map prints them (not territory).

frames.label: to 1054
frames.title: Kyivan Rus' under Volodymyr and Yaroslav, to 1054
frames.source: Same atlas map as 862-972: Rus' c.880-912, expansion c.912-972 and c.972-1054; peach = area paying tribute. Pecheneg steppe to 1036.  |  988: Christianization of Rus' under Volodymyr the Great.
frames.event: 988: Christianization of Rus' under Volodymyr the Great.

frames.label: c. 1015
frames.title: The Pontic steppes: Pecheneg Khanates (889–1091) and Rus'
frames.source: Source: 'The Pontic steppes, c. 1015' (Wikimedia Commons). Western edge is schematic. Kyiv region (Ruska zemlia) and Volhynia carried from the 862–912 frame.  |  1015: Volodymyr dies; his sons contest Kyiv (Yaroslav the Wise wins by 1036).
frames.event: 1015: Volodymyr dies; his sons contest Kyiv (Yaroslav the Wise wins by 1036).

frames.title: Principalities of Kievan Rus' and the Pecheneg Khanates
frames.source: Source: Principalities of Kievan Rus' (1054–1132), Wikimedia Commons. Steppe: Pecheneg Khanates (889–1091); no extent on the source map. Halych principality from 1141–44.  |  1054: death of Yaroslav the Wise; Rus' splits into rival principalities.
frames.event: 1054: death of Yaroslav the Wise; Rus' splits into rival principalities.

frames.title: Principalities of Kievan Rus' and the Cuman steppe
frames.source: Principalities per the 1054–1132 map; Cuman steppe per the 1130 CE Europe map (approximate); Halych principality from 1141–44.

frames.label: to 1239
frames.title: Rus' principalities and the Cuman-Kipchak steppe, on the eve of the Mongol conquest
frames.source: Source: "Kievan Rus' - Kyivan Rus' (1220–1240)", 'Historical maps of Ukraine' (licence unchecked). Steppe: Cuman-Kipchak map (1200–1241), shown until 1239; approximate.  |  1187: 'Ukraina' first appears in a chronicle (Kyiv Chronicle). 1240: Mongols destroy Kyiv. 1253: Danylo of Galicia crowned King of Rus'.
frames.event: 1187: 'Ukraina' first appears in a chronicle (Kyiv Chronicle). 1240: Mongols destroy Kyiv. 1253: Danylo of Galicia crowned King of Rus'.

frames.title: Kingdom of Rus' (Galicia–Volhynia): the strongest Rus' state after the Mongol invasion
frames.source: Source: 'The Kingdom of Galicia–Volhynia, 1245–1349' (Wikimedia Commons); schematic, so extents are approximate. Danylo crowned king 1253; Lviv founded c.1256; capital moved from Halych to Kholm and Volodymyr. Turov–Pinsk passed to Lithuania in the early 14th c.  |  1245: Danylo wins at Yaroslav and accepts Mongol suzerainty. 1253: Danylo crowned King of Rus'. c.1256: Lviv founded. 1264: Danylo dies; 1301: the Romanovych line ends; 1340: last ruler dies, Poland, Lithuania and Hungary contest the kingdom.
frames.event: 1245: Danylo wins at Yaroslav and accepts Mongol suzerainty. 1253: Danylo crowned King of Rus'. c.1256: Lviv founded. 1264: Danylo dies; 1301: the Romanovych line ends; 1340: last ruler dies, Poland, Lithuania and Hungary contest the kingdom.

frames.title: Golden Horde, Galicia-Volhynia and the Rus' principalities under Mongol suzerainty
frames.source: Steppe: Golden Horde (from 1240), extent as on the c. 1240 frame (approximate); Rus' principalities as on 1239; Hungary (Transcarpathia), Theodoro and Gazaria per the site list.  |  Kingdom of Rus' (Galicia-Volhynia, 1253-1349) carries on the Rus' tradition after the Mongol conquest.
frames.event: Kingdom of Rus' (Galicia-Volhynia, 1253-1349) carries on the Rus' tradition after the Mongol conquest.

frames.title: Lithuania's gains to 1341 (Vytenis and Gediminas) beside the Golden Horde and Galicia-Volhynia
frames.source: Lithuanian stage from the Polish wall map (Piętka) 'Wielkie Księstwo Litewskie 1240–1430'; other classes as on the 1240–1340 frame.

frames.title: Galicia taken by the Kingdom of Poland; Volhynia contested
frames.source: Casimir III's campaigns 1340–49 brought Galicia under Polish control (political control, not yet incorporation); Volhynia was contested between Lithuania and Poland. Other classes as on 1341.  |  1349: Poland takes Galicia; Volhynia passes to Lithuania.
frames.event: 1349: Poland takes Galicia; Volhynia passes to Lithuania.

frames.title: Grand Duchy of Lithuania, Kingdom of Poland and the Golden Horde
frames.source: Piętka map (Lithuania to 1377). Incorporation did not erase Rus' princely traditions, elites or law. Steppe: World Through Time 1376, approximate.  |  1362: Battle of Blue Waters; Lithuania takes Kyiv and Podolia from the Golden Horde.
frames.event: 1362: Battle of Blue Waters; Lithuania takes Kyiv and Podolia from the Golden Horde.

frames.title: Lithuanian and Polish lands, with regions
frames.source: Sources: Piętka wall map 1240–1430 (regions); Wild Fields from the 1430 Lithuania map; Golden Horde, Blue Horde (Crimea) per a 1431 online map; Theodoro from the 1434 map; Moldavia from the 1434 map.

frames.title: Lithuania under Vytautas: Kyiv and Podillia lands and the Black Sea coast
frames.source: Source: 'Grand Duchy of Lithuania (1386–1434)', Historical maps of Ukraine (licence unchecked); fit within about 10–15 km. Dark = lands of Kyiv, Chernihiv and Podillia; light green = annexed by Vytautas 1392–1430 down to Ochakiv; pale = lands disputed with Poland.  |  1392: Vytautas becomes Grand Duke (Astrava agreement). 1399: defeated by the Golden Horde at the Vorskla. 1410: Grunwald. 1430: Vytautas dies. Lithuanian rule reaches the Black Sea coast near Ochakiv.
frames.event: 1392: Vytautas becomes Grand Duke (Astrava agreement). 1399: defeated by the Golden Horde at the Vorskla. 1410: Grunwald. 1430: Vytautas dies. Lithuanian rule reaches the Black Sea coast near Ochakiv.

frames.title: Political territories and historical regions (reconstructed from historical maps)
frames.source: Voivodeships created 1434 = administrative incorporation (Polish control from 1349). East Podolia: Lithuanian sphere, shifting border. Lithuanian lands had differing status.  |  1434: Ruthenian Voivodeship (Poland) set up. 1441: Crimean Khanate formed.
frames.event: 1434: Ruthenian Voivodeship (Poland) set up. 1441: Crimean Khanate formed.

frames.title: The Crimean Khanate at its greatest extent
frames.source: Source: 'Crimean Khanate at its maximum extent' (Wikimedia Commons, after Temushev 2021); good fit to the coast. Hatched on the map = nominally Lithuanian, de facto Wild Fields. West of about 28°E the frame follows the 1434 frame.  |  1475: Crimean Khanate becomes an Ottoman vassal. 1502: Great Horde destroyed; Crimea dominates the steppe. 1523: furthest extent. Lithuania holds the Dnipro lands only nominally; Cossack groups form on the frontier.
frames.event: 1475: Crimean Khanate becomes an Ottoman vassal. 1502: Great Horde destroyed; Crimea dominates the steppe. 1523: furthest extent. Lithuania holds the Dnipro lands only nominally; Cossack groups form on the frontier.

frames.title: Poland and Lithuania at the Union of Lublin
frames.source: Regions as lettered on a 1569 atlas map. At Lublin Volhynia, Bratslav and Kyiv passed from Lithuania to the Crown. Labels, not borders.  |  1569: Union of Lublin. 1570s-80s: Zaporozhian Sich emerges. 1596: Union of Brest.
frames.event: 1569: Union of Lublin. 1570s-80s: Zaporozhian Sich emerges. 1596: Union of Brest.

frames.title: Ukrainian Cossack State of Hetman Khmelnytsky
frames.source: Extent as on a 1648-57 Hetmanate map. Arrows: Khmelnytsky campaigns 1648-53, traced by eye.  |  1648: Khmelnytsky Uprising begins. 1654: Pereiaslav agreement with Muscovy.
frames.event: 1648: Khmelnytsky Uprising begins. 1654: Pereiaslav agreement with Muscovy.

frames.title: Treaty of Hadiach: the planned Duchy of Ruthenia
frames.source: Source: Wikimedia Commons Commonwealth map of 1658 (Mathiasrex) with the 'Duchy of Ruthenia' (Kyiv, Bratslav, Chernihiv). The plan was ratified in 1659 but never carried out. Schematic in the south; fit within about 15 km.  |  1657: Khmelnytsky dies. 1658: Treaty of Hadiach, signed by Hetman Vyhovsky, proposes a Duchy of Ruthenia as a third member of the Commonwealth. Ratified 1659, never put into effect.
frames.event: 1657: Khmelnytsky dies. 1658: Treaty of Hadiach, signed by Hetman Vyhovsky, proposes a Duchy of Ruthenia as a third member of the Commonwealth. Ratified 1659, never put into effect.

frames.title: Truce of Andrusovo: Ukraine divided at the Dnipro
frames.source: Extent as on a map of the 1667 truce. Left Bank and Kyiv to Russia (Kyiv confirmed 1686); Zaporizhia a joint condominium. Hetmanates not shown.  |  1667: Truce of Andrusovo. 1686: Eternal Peace confirms the Dnipro division and cedes Kyiv.
frames.event: 1667: Truce of Andrusovo. 1686: Eternal Peace confirms the Dnipro division and cedes Kyiv.

frames.title: Ottoman Podillia: the Right Bank under Ottoman pressure
frames.source: Podillia from the Shepherd map 'The Ottoman Empire 1481–1683' (coarse, about 50 km); rest as on the 1667 frame. Ottoman from 1672 (Kamianets), returned to Poland at Karlowitz in 1699. The Right Bank was devastated (the Ruin).  |  1672: Ottomans take Kamianets; Treaty of Buchach cedes Podillia. 1676: Hetman Doroshenko surrenders Chyhyryn. 1686: Eternal Peace confirms Kyiv for Russia. 1699: Treaty of Karlowitz returns Podillia to Poland.
frames.event: 1672: Ottomans take Kamianets; Treaty of Buchach cedes Podillia. 1676: Hetman Doroshenko surrenders Chyhyryn. 1686: Eternal Peace confirms Kyiv for Russia. 1699: Treaty of Karlowitz returns Podillia to Poland.

frames.title: The Eternal Peace of 1686
frames.source: Source: Wikimedia Commons map 'Rzeczpospolita w 1686' (Mathiasrex). Russia keeps the Left Bank and Kyiv; Podillia is Ottoman (1672–99); the Right Bank stays Polish.  |  1686: Eternal Peace between Russia and Poland-Lithuania: Russia keeps the Left Bank and Kyiv for good. 1699: Karlowitz returns Podillia to Poland.
frames.event: 1686: Eternal Peace between Russia and Poland-Lithuania: Russia keeps the Left Bank and Kyiv for good. 1699: Karlowitz returns Podillia to Poland.

frames.title: Homann's map 'Ukrania quae et Terra Cosaccorum'
frames.source: Regions as coloured on a 1716 map (Homann); extents approximate. Right Bank Polish after 1699; Left Bank under Russia; Zaporozhia under Crimean protection.  |  1709: Battle of Poltava; Mazepa and Charles XII defeated. The Sich passes under Crimean protection (1709-34).
frames.event: 1709: Battle of Poltava; Mazepa and Charles XII defeated. The Sich passes under Crimean protection (1709-34).

frames.title: Zaporozhia under Russian protection, and the lands it lost
frames.source: Source: 'Zaporizhzhia in the 18th century' (Terechenko, 2018), georeferenced by city points (error about 15–25 km). Yellow = Sich lands; the Nova Serbia (1752–64) and Slavo-Serbia (1753–64) strips were cut from them. South-east strip (lost to the Don Cossacks, 1747) is approximate.  |  1734: the Zaporozhian Host returns under Russian protection and founds the New Sich (Pidpilna). 1747: border with the Don Cossacks drawn. 1752–53: Nova Serbia and Slavo-Serbia cut from Zaporozhian lands. 1764: Hetmanate abolished. 1775: Sich destroyed.
frames.event: 1734: the Zaporozhian Host returns under Russian protection and founds the New Sich (Pidpilna). 1747: border with the Don Cossacks drawn. 1752–53: Nova Serbia and Slavo-Serbia cut from Zaporozhian lands. 1764: Hetmanate abolished. 1775: Sich destroyed.

frames.title: Cossack lands c. 1745: Hetmanate, Zaporozhia and Sloboda Ukraine
frames.source: Source: 'The Ukrainian lands in the Russian Empire, 1740–1750' (Wikimedia Commons), drawn on modern Ukraine. Hetmanate = Left Bank only. Compare with 1649: the Cossack state has shrunk to a fraction.  |  1764: Catherine II abolishes the Hetmanate and the post of hetman. 1775: Zaporozhian Sich destroyed. Cossack lands shrink: 1649 → 1667 (split at the Dnipro) → 1740s (Left Bank, Sloboda and Sich) → gone by 1775.
frames.event: 1764: Catherine II abolishes the Hetmanate and the post of hetman. 1775: Zaporozhian Sich destroyed. Cossack lands shrink: 1649 → 1667 (split at the Dnipro) → 1740s (Left Bank, Sloboda and Sich) → gone by 1775.

frames.title: First Partition of Poland
frames.source: Austria takes Galicia-Lodomeria (Lviv, Przemysl). Shapes traced from a partitions map; Left Bank and the south as before.  |  1764: Hetmanate abolished. 1772: first partition. 1775: Zaporozhian Sich destroyed.
frames.event: 1764: Hetmanate abolished. 1772: first partition. 1775: Zaporozhian Sich destroyed.

frames.title: Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca: the Crimean Khanate 'independent'
frames.source: Schematic: the treaty map is not to scale, so extents here follow the treaty text. Crimea formally independent (annexed 1783); Russia gets Kinburn with a strip between the Dnipro and the Southern Buh, Kerch and Yenikale, and Azov.  |  1774: Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca. The Crimean Khanate becomes 'independent' under Russian influence; Russia gains Kinburn, Kerch, Yenikale and Azov. 1783: Crimea annexed.
frames.event: 1774: Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca. The Crimean Khanate becomes 'independent' under Russian influence; Russia gains Kinburn, Kerch, Yenikale and Azov. 1783: Crimea annexed.

frames.title: Second Partition of Poland
frames.source: Russia takes the Right Bank: Kyiv, Bratslav and Podolia, E. Volhynia. Crimea (1783) and Yedysan (1792) already Russian; Bukovina Austrian since 1774-75.  |  1783: Russia annexes Crimea. 1792: Yedysan to Russia. 1793: second partition.
frames.event: 1783: Russia annexes Crimea. 1792: Yedysan to Russia. 1793: second partition.

frames.title: Third Partition of Poland
frames.source: Russia takes W. Volhynia (Lutsk); Austria takes West Galicia (Chelm land, Krakow). The Commonwealth ends.

frames.title: After the Treaty of Bucharest: Ukrainian lands in the Russian and Austrian empires
frames.source: States of the gazetteer (the states-animation page of the project), shown on the grid; the most specific state that holds a cell. Russia takes Bessarabia (Budjak) in 1812. Galicia, Bukovina and Transcarpathia are Habsburg.  |  1795–1815: Ukrainian lands pass to Russia and Austria. 1812: Treaty of Bucharest gives Russia Bessarabia.
frames.event: 1795–1815: Ukrainian lands pass to Russia and Austria. 1812: Treaty of Bucharest gives Russia Bessarabia.

frames.title: On the eve of the First World War
frames.source: States of the gazetteer. Russian Empire (Little Russia, Sloboda, Novorossiya, Taurida), Austrian Galicia and Bukovina, Hungarian Transcarpathia, Romanian Bessarabia is Russian.  |  1863 Valuev circular and 1876 Ems decree restrict Ukrainian print in Russia; Galicia is the centre of the national movement. 1914: war begins.
frames.event: 1863 Valuev circular and 1876 Ems decree restrict Ukrainian print in Russia; Galicia is the centre of the national movement. 1914: war begins.

frames.title: The Provisional Government and the Central Rada
frames.source: States of the gazetteer. After the February Revolution the Russian Republic holds the Ukrainian governorates; the Central Rada (Kyiv) proclaims the UNR in November 1917.  |  Feb 1917: revolution; Central Rada formed in Kyiv. Nov 1917: UNR proclaimed (Third Universal).
frames.event: Feb 1917: revolution; Central Rada formed in Kyiv. Nov 1917: UNR proclaimed (Third Universal).

frames.title: Ukrainian State and the West Ukrainian People's Republic
frames.source: States of the gazetteer, late 1918. Hetman Skoropadsky's state (April–December); the ZUNR proclaimed in Lviv on 1 November; Rusyn councils in Transcarpathia.  |  Apr 1918: Hetman Skoropadsky takes power. 1 Nov: ZUNR proclaimed in Lviv. Dec: the Directorate overthrows the Hetmanate.
frames.event: Apr 1918: Hetman Skoropadsky takes power. 1 Nov: ZUNR proclaimed in Lviv. Dec: the Directorate overthrows the Hetmanate.

frames.title: The Ukrainian People's Republic, the Soviets and Poland
frames.source: States of the gazetteer, spring 1919. UNR (Directorate) and ZUNR united on 22 January; Bolshevik, White and Polish forces advance; Hutsul Republic and Free Territory.  |  22 Jan 1919: act of union of UNR and ZUNR. War of the UNR with Bolsheviks, Whites and Poland.
frames.event: 22 Jan 1919: act of union of UNR and ZUNR. War of the UNR with Bolsheviks, Whites and Poland.

frames.title: After the Treaty of Riga: Ukraine divided
frames.source: States of the gazetteer. Soviet Ukraine (the Ukrainian SSR, part of the USSR from December 1922); Poland holds Galicia and Volhynia; Romania holds Northern Bukovina and Bessarabia; Czechoslovakia holds Subcarpathian Rus.  |  1921: Treaty of Riga. 1922: Ukrainian SSR joins the USSR. 1923: Ukrainization policy begins.
frames.event: 1921: Treaty of Riga. 1922: Ukrainian SSR joins the USSR. 1923: Ukrainization policy begins.

frames.title: After 1939–40: Western Ukraine joins Soviet Ukraine
frames.source: States of the gazetteer. The USSR takes Galicia and Volhynia (September 1939), then Northern Bukovina and Southern Bessarabia (1940).  |  Sept 1939: USSR enters Poland. 1940: Northern Bukovina and Bessarabia annexed.
frames.event: Sept 1939: USSR enters Poland. 1940: Northern Bukovina and Bessarabia annexed.

frames.title: Occupation, 1941–44: Reichskommissariat Ukraine and other regimes
frames.source: States of the gazetteer. German invasion from 22 June 1941. Reichskommissariat Ukraine (civil administration from September 1941); District Galicia in the General Government (from August 1941); Romanian Transnistria, with Romania also holding Northern Bukovina and Bessarabia; Hungarian Transcarpathia (since 1939). Crimea and much of the east stayed under German military administration.  |  22 Jun 1941: German invasion. 1941–44: German and Romanian occupation; the Holocaust; OUN and UPA.
frames.event: 22 Jun 1941: German invasion. 1941–44: German and Romanian occupation; the Holocaust; OUN and UPA.

frames.title: Soviet Ukraine after the Second World War
frames.source: States of the gazetteer. Transcarpathia joins Soviet Ukraine in 1946; Crimea is a Russian SFSR oblast until 1954.  |  1944–46: Soviet Ukraine regains its lands; 1946 Transcarpathia. 1954: Crimea transferred.
frames.event: 1944–46: Soviet Ukraine regains its lands; 1946 Transcarpathia. 1954: Crimea transferred.

frames.label: 1 December 1991
frames.title: Independent Ukraine
frames.source: States of the gazetteer. Independence declared 24 August 1991; referendum 1 December 1991. Crimea, Donetsk and Luhansk: Ukrainian territory.  |  24 Aug 1991: independence; 1 Dec: referendum (over 90%).
frames.event: 24 Aug 1991: independence; 1 Dec: referendum (over 90%).

frames.title: Crimea and parts of Donetsk and Luhansk occupied by Russia
frames.source: States of the gazetteer. Russia occupied Crimea in 2014 and, with proxy 'DNR/LNR' formations, parts of Donetsk and Luhansk. This is Ukrainian territory unlawfully occupied by Russia.  |  2014: Euromaidan; Russia occupies Crimea (Feb–Mar) and starts war in Donbas.
frames.event: 2014: Euromaidan; Russia occupies Crimea (Feb–Mar) and starts war in Donbas.

frames.label: 24 February 2022
frames.title: The full-scale Russian invasion begins
frames.source: States of the gazetteer. On 24 February 2022 Russia already occupied Crimea and, with proxy 'DNR/LNR' formations, parts of Donetsk and Luhansk. This is Ukrainian territory unlawfully occupied by Russia.  |  24 Feb 2022: full-scale Russian invasion.
frames.event: 24 Feb 2022: full-scale Russian invasion.

frames.title: After the full-scale invasion of 2022
frames.source: States of the gazetteer. Russia occupies Crimea and larger parts of the south and east; its annexation claims of 2022 are not recognised. The line between the two regions is the approximate extent of occupation; Ukraine’s internationally recognised borders are unchanged.  |  24 Feb 2022: full-scale Russian invasion.
frames.event: 24 Feb 2022: full-scale Russian invasion.
